hook: An FBI case file section spanning 1950–1952 that compiles OSI-FBI liaison memos, Air Force scientific investigation records on green fireballs and discs near sensitive New Mexico installations, an anomalous physical-trace incident reported by Philadelphia police, and unsolicited public correspondence to J. Edgar Hoover claiming flying saucer theories were stolen by a government physicist.
why_it_matters: This section documents the moment the U.S. government formalized its scientific response to unexplained aerial phenomena near nuclear sites, including the Air Force's contract with Land-Air, Inc. to establish observation posts—a precursor to what became Project Twinkle. The simultaneous presence of a Soviet missile hypothesis (Dr. LaPaz estimating Ural-to-New Mexico transit under 15 minutes) and an unexplained physical-trace case in Philadelphia illustrates how early investigators held multiple competing explanations open. The FBI's role as a routing and liaison body, forwarding public and inter-agency reports to OSI and Air Force Intelligence, reveals the distributed and ad hoc character of early UAP information management.

key_findings.finding: The Air Force had recorded approximately 150 observations of anomalous aerial phenomena near sensitive New Mexico installations since December 1948, formally classifying them into three types: green fireballs, discs, and meteoric objects.

quotes.text: Observations of aerial phenomena occurring within the vicinity of sensitive installations have been recorded by the Air Force since December, 1948. The phenomena have been classified into 3 general types which are identified as follows: 1. Green fireballs, objects moving at high speed in shapes resembling half moons, circles and discs emitting green light. &. Discs, round flat shaped objects or phenomena moving at fast velocity and emitting a brilliant white light or reflected light. 3. Meteors, aerial phenomena resembling meteoric material moving at high velocity and varying in color.

Since 1948, approximately 150 observations of aerial phenomena referred to above have been recorded in the vicinity of installations in New Merico. A number of observations have been reported by different reliable individuals at approximately the same time.

key_findings.finding: Meteor expert Dr. Lincoln LaPaz, after concluding roughly half the phenomena were meteoric, raised the hypothesis that the remainder could be Soviet guided missiles launched from the Ural region, capable of reaching New Mexico in under 15 minutes.

quotes.text: He concluded, as a result of his investigation, that approrimately half of the phenomena recorded were of meteoric origin. The other phenomena commonly referred to as green fireballs or discs he believed to be U.S. guided missiles being tested in the neighborhood of the installations.

missiles moving with the velocities of the order of those found for the green fireballs and discs could travel from the Ural region of the USSR to New Mexico in less than 15 minutes. He suggested that the observations might be of guided missiles launched from bases in the Urals.

key_findings.finding: The Air Force contracted Land-Air, Incorporated of Alamogordo to establish scientific observation posts near Vaughn, New Mexico specifically to photograph and measure the green fireball and disc phenomena—a formal instrumented monitoring program.

quotes.text: The Air Force together with Land-Air, Incorporated, have established a number of observation posts in the vicinity of Vaughn, New Mexico, for the purpose of photographing and determining the speed, height and nature of the unusual Phenomena referred to as green fireballs and discs. On May 24, 1950, personnel of Land-Air, Incorporated, sighted 8 to 10 objects of aerial phenomena.
OSI has contracted with Land-Air Inc., Alamogordo, New Merico, to make scientific study of the unerplained phenomena.

key_findings.finding: Philadelphia police officers in September 1950 reported an unidentified object that descended to tree-top level, emitted a purplish glow described as almost a mist, completely disintegrated over 25 minutes when touched, left an odorless residue, and was so light it did not bend the vegetation where it landed—a physical-trace case routed to the FBI and then OSI.

key_findings.finding: A Virginia civilian, Mrs. Nellie T. Dull, wrote simultaneously to Air Force Intelligence, the FBI, and the Justice Department in August 1952 alleging physicist Noel Scott had plagiarized her flying saucer theory, and speculating that the solution could enable man-made flying saucers usable with nuclear weapons or for moon travel—illustrating the volume and character of unsolicited public UFO correspondence routed through the Bureau.

legacy_program_connections.reasoning: The systematic Air Force investigation of green fireballs and discs near New Mexico installations documented here directly precedes and feeds into the formal Project Blue Book investigative apparatus, with OSI, Land-Air Inc., and Dr. LaPaz's involvement representing the institutional infrastructure Blue Book inherited.

The Air Force investigation chain referenced throughout this file, including OSI coordination and the forwarding of reports to Air Force Intelligence and the Pentagon, implicates Wright-Patterson as the hub for Air Force UFO analytical work during this period.

The repeated emphasis on phenomena occurring near 'sensitive installations' in New Mexico—context pointing to Los Alamos and Sandia—positions nuclear facility security as the primary driver of OSI's concern and the scientific monitoring program.

The New Mexico installations explicitly cited as sites of concern align with Sandia National Laboratories and nearby Kirtland Air Force Base, which were among the sensitive facilities the OSI was tasked to protect from aerial surveillance.
